analysis_steps.goal: Calculate polarised intensity, polarisation angles, and sub-region statistics

method.value: Compute polarised intensity PI = sqrt(Q^2 + U^2) (without debiasing at high SNR), apply a 6 mJy/beam threshold, compute polarisation angles theta = 0.5 arctan(U/Q) and uncertainties delta_theta = 0.5 * delta_Q / PI, and calculate mean and median angles in 5 defined sub-regions.

evidence.quote: The mean and median polarisation angles, as well as the number of independent measurements, in each region are listed in Table 1.

key_parameters.value: PI threshold >= 6 mJy/beam; delta_Q = delta_U = 0.62 mJy/beam; delta_theta <= 3.0 deg

analysis_steps.goal: Compare observed polarisation geometries in sub-regions against geometric models using Monte Carlo KS and Kuiper tests

method.value: Predict pixel-by-pixel polarisation angles for geometric models (uniform 26 deg E of N, concentric around BN/KL, concentric around Source I, concentric around ring feature), perturb model angles with Gaussian noise of width sigma_theta (1 to 20 deg) 1000 times per sigma_theta, and run two-sided KS and Kuiper tests against observed angle distributions.

evidence.quote: We quantified the similarity of these models to the data using two-sided Kolmorogov-Smirnov (KS) and Kuiper tests.
For each model, we determined polarisation angles predicted in each pixel by the model, and drew sets of perturbations on these angles from a Gaussian distribution of width $\sigma_{\theta}$.
We repeated this process 1000 times for each value of $\sigma_{\theta}$ considered. We tested $\sigma_{\theta}$ values in the range $1^{\circ} - 20^{\circ}$.

key_parameters.value: sigma_theta in range 1 deg - 20 deg; 1000 Monte Carlo realisations per sigma_theta; consistency criterion p > 0.05

evidence.quote: We repeated this process 1000 times for each value of $\sigma_{\theta}$ considered. We tested $\sigma_{\theta}$ values in the range $1^{\circ} - 20^{\circ}$.
According to both tests, the BN/KL-concentric model is the only model that can be made consistent ($p > 0.05$) with the data in the eastern arm

analysis_steps.goal: Estimate characteristic grain alignment and damping timescales in the Anomalous Region/Fork

method.value: Analytically evaluate and compare the Larmor precession timescale (tau_Lar), mechanical alignment timescale (tau_mech), radiative precession timescale (tau_rad,p), and gas damping timescale (tau_gas) as functions of grain size a.

evidence.quote: We consider these hypotheses in turn below, and then as a check on our analysis confirm that the gas damping timescale is sufficiently long in the region to allow a preferential dust precession axis to exist.
$\tau_{gas}< \tau_{rad,p}$ holds only for unphysically small grains, with $a_{-5} < 10^{-10}$, at which size $\tau_{Lar} \ll \tau_{gas}$ would hold if such grains existed.
and so we adopt $\hat{B}\sim 2000$.

assumptions.value: Paramagnetic grains with rho = 3 g cm^-3, axial ratio s = 0.5; unobscured radiation from Source I with anisotropy gamma ~ 1 and RAT efficiency |Q_Gamma| <= 0.4; thermal grain rotation (omega ~ omega_th); subsonic drift (Delta v < c_s) for v-MATs.

evidence.quote: (cite: draine1996) gives values for magnetic susceptibility $\chi(0)$ in the range $4.2\times 10^{-5}-4.2\times10^{-3}$ for paramagnetic grains, and so we take $\hat{\chi}\sim 0.4-40$.

As we are specifically considering the radiation field from Source I, which we expect to be strongly anisotropic, we take $\gamma\sim 1$. Note that this implies that radiation from Source I is effectively unobscured in the western arm of the Fork; a justifiable assumption if the polarised emission indeed arises from the Source I outflow cavity wall, which we discuss further below. We further take $|{Q_{\Gamma}}| \leq 0.4$ (cite: lazarian2007a; tazaki2017), and so $\gamma|{Q_{\Gamma}}|/0.01 \lesssim 40$.

validation.value: Check that the gas damping timescale tau_gas is longer than precession timescales across physically plausible grain sizes

evidence.quote: Thus grains in the Fork cannot have their alignments randomised by gas collisions faster than they can be induced to precess around either the magnetic field direction or the radiation anisotropy gradient by RATs.

findings_qualitative.value: In Orion Source I, unresolved Band 7 polarisation is parallel to the disc minor axis and likely arises from dust self-scattering in the optically thick, nearly edge-on disc, although the geometry is degenerate with concentric polarisation around BN/KL.

evidence.quote: In Source I, we found an unresolved polarisation geometry parallel to the minor axis of the Source I disc, consistent with polarisation arising from dust self-scattering. The Source I disc is optically thick and viewed almost edge-on, supporting this interpretation; however, the predicted polarisation pattern is degenerate with that for a polarisation pattern concentric around the centre of the BN/KL explosion.

findings_qualitative.value: In the eastern arm of the Fork and in MF4/MF5, the polarisation geometry is concentric around the BN/KL explosion centre, tracing a magnetic field reordered into a radial configuration by the explosion.

evidence.quote: In the eastern arm of the Anomalous Region/Fork, we found a polarisation geometry consistent with being concentric around the centre of the BN/KL explosion, consistent with the magnetic field having been reordered to be radial around the BN/KL explosion, as posited by (cite: tang2010) and (cite: cortes2020).

In MF4/MF5, we found a polarisation geometry consistent with being concentric around the BN/KL explosion centre, and so tracing a magnetic field that has been reordered to be radial around the BN/KL explosion.

findings_qualitative.value: In the western arm of the Fork, polarisation is concentric around Source I; moderately large grains (> 0.005-0.1 um) in unobscured outflow cavity walls may be aligned by k-RATs driven by Source I's radiation, or alternatively aligned by B-RATs tracing gas infall onto the Main Ridge.

evidence.quote: While our estimates of both timescales are highly uncertain, we find $\tau_{rad,p}<\tau_{Lar}$ for moderately large grains ($>0.005-0.1\,\mu$m), suggesting that grains in this region may be aligned by radiative torques to precess around the radiation anisotropy gradient (k-RATs), i.e. to be perpendicular to the gradient of intensity from Source I.
Alternatively, the grains may continue to precess around the magnetic field direction (B-RATs), and so could trace infall of material onto the Main Ridge/Hot Core region.

findings_qualitative.value: In the Main Ridge, grains remain aligned by B-RATs perpendicular to the large-scale magnetic field, likely because the dense gas in the Ridge has resisted disruption by the BN/KL explosion and high extinction shields the Ridge from Source I's radiation.

evidence.quote: In the Main Ridge, we found a polarisation geometry consistent with that of the large-scale magnetic field in the region, and so determined that grains are aligned perpendicular to the magnetic field (B-RAT alignment).

The consistency with the large-scale magnetic field, despite recent findings that the magnetic field is energetically subdominant compared to the BN/KL outflow, may result from the field being well-coupled to gas in the Ridge that has not been disrupted by the BN/KL explosion.

findings_qualitative.value: In the Compact Ridge/MF1, the polarisation geometry is broadly similar to that of the large-scale magnetic field but shows ordered deviation (turning south at the periphery), possibly merging into the large-scale hourglass field of OMC-1.

evidence.quote: In the Compact Ridge/MF1, likely located sufficiently far from the BN/KL explosion and Source I to remain uninfluenced by their effects, we found a polarisation geometry similar to, but showing ordered deviation from, being perpendicular to the large-scale magnetic field direction. The field may here be merging into the large-scale ‘hourglass’ field identified in single-dish observations.

claims.hypothesis: Polarisation in the Orion Source I disc arises from dust self-scattering.
claims.experiment: Measure the unresolved ALMA Band 7 polarisation angle over Source I and compare it with the disc minor axis, large-scale magnetic field, and BN/KL-concentric models, alongside literature constraints on optical depth and inclination.
claims.result: Mean polarisation angle is 53.5 +/- 8.6 deg (median 52.0 +/- 5.4 deg), matching the disc minor axis (53 deg) of an inclined (i > 74 deg), optically thick disc, though also consistent with a BN/KL-concentric pattern.
claims.finding: Dust self-scattering is the probable source of the observed polarisation in Source I, implying grain growth to ~140 um (and <500 um given 3.1 mm upper limits), though the pattern is geometrically degenerate with being concentric around BN/KL.

evidence.quote: While we note that the polarisation geometry is also consistent with being concentric around BN/KL, dust self-scattering is an established mechanism for producing polarisation in protostellar discs, the necessary conditions for which are matched in Source I, and so we consider it to be the probable source of the dust polarisation which we observe.

The Source I disc is optically thick and viewed almost edge-on, supporting this interpretation; however, the predicted polarisation pattern is degenerate with that for a polarisation pattern concentric around the centre of the BN/KL explosion.

claims.hypothesis: Polarisation in the western arm of the Anomalous Region/Fork is caused by radiative alignment torques precessing around the radiation anisotropy vector of Source I (k-RATs).
claims.experiment: Perform Monte Carlo KS and Kuiper tests comparing observed polarisation angles to concentric geometric models, and analytically calculate Larmor, radiative precession, mechanical alignment, and gas damping timescales.
claims.result: Only the Source-I-concentric model is consistent (p > 0.05 for sigma_theta < 5-8 deg) with the western arm data, and tau_rad,p < tau_Lar holds for grain radii a > 0.005 - 0.1 um if radiation from Source I is unobscured.
claims.finding: Grains > 0.005-0.1 um in the western arm of the Fork may be aligned by k-RATs driven by Source I in the outflow cavity walls, though B-RAT alignment in infalling gas cannot be ruled out.

evidence.quote: According to both tests, the BN/KL-concentric model is the only model that can be made consistent ($p > 0.05$) with the data in the eastern arm, while the Source-I-concentric model is the only model that can be made consistent with the data in the western arm.

While our estimates of both timescales are highly uncertain, we find $\tau_{rad,p}<\tau_{Lar}$ for moderately large grains ($>0.005-0.1\,\mu$m), suggesting that grains in this region may be aligned by radiative torques to precess around the radiation anisotropy gradient (k-RATs), i.e. to be perpendicular to the gradient of intensity from Source I.
We cannot rule out either k-RAT or B-RAT alignment as having produced the observed polarisation geometry.

claims.hypothesis: Subsonic mechanical alignment torques (v-MATs) or supersonic Gold alignment cause the polarisation geometry in the Anomalous Region/Fork.
claims.experiment: Compare predicted Gold alignment geometries to observed vectors and compare the v-MAT mechanical precession timescale tau_mech to the Larmor timescale tau_Lar.
claims.result: Gold alignment predicts radial or outflow-parallel vectors (inconsistent with observations), and tau_mech >= 72 (omega/omega_th) yr >> tau_Lar ~ 1.6(10^-5 - 10^-3) a_-5^2 yr unless grains rotate subthermally (omega << omega_th).
claims.finding: Both Gold alignment and subsonic v-MATs are ruled out or shown to be unlikely as the main cause of grain alignment in the Fork.

evidence.quote: All of these geometries are inconsistent with the observed polarisation pattern shown in Figure 3, and so we do not consider Gold alignment further.
The timescale for v-MAT alignment thus remains too long for this mechanism to be likely to be the main cause of grain alignment in the Fork.

claims.hypothesis: The magnetic field in the eastern arm of the Fork and in MF4/MF5 has been dragged into a radial configuration around the BN/KL explosion centre, whereas the Main Ridge retains the large-scale magnetic field orientation.
claims.experiment: Test observed polarisation angle distributions in the eastern arm of the Fork, MF4/MF5, and the Main Ridge against the BN/KL-concentric, Source-I-concentric, and large-scale field (26 deg E of N) models using KS and Kuiper tests.
claims.result: The BN/KL-concentric model is the only consistent model (p > 0.05, best fit sigma_theta ~ 8 deg) in the eastern arm of the Fork and MF4/MF5, while the 26 deg E of N model is the only consistent model (best fit sigma_theta = 8 deg) in the Main Ridge.
claims.finding: The magnetic field has been reordered to be radial around the BN/KL explosion in the eastern Fork and MF4/MF5, while the Main Ridge resists disruption by the explosion and retains B-RAT alignment with the large-scale field.

evidence.quote: There is no angular dispersion value at which the polarisation pattern in the Ridge is consistent with being concentric around either the centre of the BN/KL explosion or around Source I, suggesting that the grains remain aligned by B-RATs to be perpendicular to the large-scale magnetic field.

In the eastern arm of the Anomalous Region/Fork, we found a polarisation geometry consistent with being concentric around the centre of the BN/KL explosion, consistent with the magnetic field having been reordered to be radial around the BN/KL explosion, as posited by (cite: tang2010) and (cite: cortes2020).

In MF4/MF5, we found a polarisation geometry consistent with being concentric around the BN/KL explosion centre, and so tracing a magnetic field that has been reordered to be radial around the BN/KL explosion.

why_this_data.value: ALMA Band 7 (881 um) polarimetry provides high spatial resolution and sensitivity in dense, high-mass star-forming gas around Source I to test whether a single grain alignment mechanism explains the complex polarisation morphology.

evidence.quote: The polarimetric capabilities of the new generation of submillimetre telescopes, including the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), have made magnetic fields in dense, star-forming gas newly accessible (cite: cortes2016; kwon2019).

In this paper we present ALMA Band 7 (0.88mm) observations of Source I and its surroundings, a subset of the area observed by (cite: cortes2020). We investigate whether a single model, or a single grain alignment mechanism, is sufficient to explain the complex polarisation morphology observed in the vicinity of Source I.

why_this_method.value: Two-sided Kolmogorov-Smirnov test was chosen as the most widely-used distribution comparison statistic, and the Kuiper test was chosen as a more appropriate similarity measure for cyclic variables (angles).

evidence.quote: We chose the KS test as the most widely-used statistic for comparing the similarity of two distributions, and the Kuiper test as a more appropriate measure of similarity for distributions of cyclic variables (cite: aizawa2020).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Calculating polarisation fractions (P = PI / I) was rejected because the Stokes I map is much more dynamic-range-limited than Stokes Q and U, which would produce artificially large polarisation fractions.

evidence.quote: We do not calculate polarisation fractions in this work, as the Stokes $I$ map is much more dynamic-range-limited than are the Stokes $Q$ and $U$ maps, as shown in Figure 2, and so any calculation of polarisation fraction is likely to produce artificially large values, particularly in low-surface-brightness regions.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Analysing the 12CO J=3->2 spectral window (spw3) was excluded because CO emission in outflows can be polarised by the Goldreich-Kylafis effect.

evidence.quote: CO emission in outflows can be polarised up to a maximum of $\sim 3$% by the Goldreich-Kylafis effect (GK effect; (cite: goldreich1982; ching2016)), which has previously been observed in OMC-1 (cite: houde2013). Data from the spectral window dedicated to imaging this line (spw3) is therefore not considered in this work.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Rotating 'pseudo-disk' with a toroidal magnetic field in OMC-1 (proposed by Tang et al. 2010) was rejected based on ALMA studies of clump distances and velocities.

evidence.quote: We consider this hypothesis to have been disfavoured by ALMA studies better determining the line-of-sight distances and velocities of the various OMC-1 clumps (cite: pagani2017).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Dust self-scattering in the western arm of the Fork was discounted because growing or entraining ~140 um grains into the outflow without destruction is unlikely.

evidence.quote: However, transport of such large dust grains, as well as their avoiding destruction in the outflow in sufficient number to produce the observed polarisation pattern, does not seem likely (cite: giacalone2019). We thus discount this hypothesis, while noting that we cannot definitively rule it out.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Supersonic mechanical (Gold) alignment in the Fork was rejected because it predicts radial or outflow-parallel polarisation patterns inconsistent with the observations.

evidence.quote: All of these geometries are inconsistent with the observed polarisation pattern shown in Figure 3, and so we do not consider Gold alignment further.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Subsonic mechanical alignment torques (v-MATs) in the Fork were rejected because the mechanical alignment timescale is much longer than the Larmor timescale unless grains rotate subthermally.

evidence.quote: The timescale for v-MAT alignment thus remains too long for this mechanism to be likely to be the main cause of grain alignment in the Fork.

limitations_admitted.value: Stokes I map is dynamic-range-limited compared to Stokes Q and U, preventing reliable calculation of polarisation fractions.

evidence.quote: We do not calculate polarisation fractions in this work, as the Stokes $I$ map is much more dynamic-range-limited than are the Stokes $Q$ and $U$ maps, as shown in Figure 2, and so any calculation of polarisation fraction is likely to produce artificially large values, particularly in low-surface-brightness regions.

limitations_admitted.value: Source I is unresolved (< 2 independent beams), and its minor-axis polarisation direction is degenerate with a BN/KL-concentric polarisation pattern.

evidence.quote: Source I is effectively unresolved in our observations. We associate six Nyquist-sampled pixels (less than two independent measurements) with the source.

The Source I disc is optically thick and viewed almost edge-on, supporting this interpretation; however, the predicted polarisation pattern is degenerate with that for a polarisation pattern concentric around the centre of the BN/KL explosion.

limitations_admitted.value: Estimates of Larmor and radiative precession timescales have large uncertainties (e.g., two orders of magnitude or more in magnetic susceptibility chi, unknown super-paramagnetic inclusions, and uncertain extinction/obscuration), preventing a definitive distinction between k-RAT and B-RAT alignment in the Fork.

evidence.quote: The uncertainty on $\tau_{Lar}$ is thus difficult to quantify: (cite: cortes2020) give a formal uncertainty on $B$ of $\sim 20$%, but this is dwarfed by the two orders of magnitude (or larger) uncertainty on $\chi$ (cite: draine1996), and so we consider only the latter when estimating the range of plausible values of $\tau_{Lar}$.

evidence.loc: Discussion of grain alignment in the Anomalous Region/Fork
evidence.quote: We emphasise that our estimates of both $\tau_{rad,p}$ and $\tau_{Lar}$ are highly uncertain. We do not have enough information to definitively identify grains in the Fork as being aligned either by k-RATs or by B-RATs.

referee_caveats_inferred: Continuum windows spw0-2 in the Orion Hot Core and OMC-1 contain rich molecular line forests; although the authors assume line polarisation is negligible in spw0-2, unsubtracted weakly polarised lines or line-wing contamination could bias Stokes Q and U in specific sub-regions.

The KS and Kuiper tests are performed on 0.25'' pixels, which oversample the 0.54'' x 0.43'' beam by ~3-4 pixels per beam; pixel-to-pixel correlations in the noise and signal may affect the nominal p-values of the two-sample tests.

data_public_as_stated.value: Available in the ALMA Science Archive under project code 2018.1.01162.S

evidence.quote: The data used in this paper are available in the ALMA Science Archive, under project code 2018.1.01162.S.
